lead: Digital electronics begins with one question: how does a wire carry a number? This unit answers it, from binary codes and 2's complement, through Boolean gates and K-maps, to adders, multiplexers, flip-flops and finally the microprocessor and microcontroller. After it you can convert and subtract in binary and BCD, minimize and build a logic circuit, use a multiplexer to implement an expression, and explain what sits inside a microcontroller chip.
about: The unit starts with the raw material: bits. Chapter 5.1 builds binary, hex, 2's complement and BCD, and shows how a machine subtracts by adding. Chapter 5.2 turns bit patterns into Boolean gates and gives the identities that shrink a circuit; 5.3 makes that shrinking systematic with minterms, maxterms and K-maps. Chapter 5.4 uses gates to build half adders, full adders and the BCD adder, the unit's first real combinational block. Chapter 5.5 shows multiplexers and demultiplexers as selectors and as a way to implement any expression. Chapter 5.6 adds one-bit memory with flip-flops, and 5.7 zooms out to the microprocessor and microcontroller, where all of it sits on one chip.

chapters.idea: Every number a digital circuit touches is a pattern of bits, and binary, octal, hex, 2's complement and BCD are only different reading rules for the same pattern.
chapters.depth: Place value in base r; base-r to decimal by weights, decimal to binary, octal or hex by repeated division with remainders read upward. Binary to octal in groups of 3 bits and binary to hex in groups of 4 bits, grouping from the decimal point outward and padding with zeros. Range of an n-bit unsigned number: 0 to 2ⁿ−1. Sign-magnitude, 1's complement, and why 2's complement won (one zero, subtraction by addition). Forming the 2's complement: invert every bit and add 1. Subtraction A − B as A plus the 2's complement of B, final carry thrown away; overflow when the carries into and out of the sign bit differ. BCD 8421 code, the six invalid codes 1010 to 1111, and BCD addition with the 0110 (add-6) correction for any nibble above 9 or producing a carry. Keep arithmetic to 4-bit and 8-bit words.

figure.title: BCD addition of 8 + 7 with the add-6 correction
figure.aria: Five 8-bit rows: 8 and 7 in BCD, their binary sum 0000 1111, the 0110 correction added to the low nibble, and the final 0001 0101 which is BCD 15.

chapters.example: Subtract 45 − 78 in 8-bit 2's complement, and add the BCD numbers 8 + 7. Now 45 = 0010 1101 and 78 = 0100 1110, so the 2's complement of 78 is 1011 0010. Adding: 0010 1101 + 1011 0010 = 1101 1111 with carry-out 0. Read as a 2's complement number, 1101 1111 is −33, and 45 − 78 = −33. BCD: 1000 + 0111 = 1111, which is greater than 9, so add 0110 to get 1111 + 0110 = 1 0101, that is the two nibbles 0001 0101 = 15.
chapters.trap: Reading a 2's complement pattern as unsigned (calling 1101 1111 '223' instead of −33), and adding the 0110 correction to every nibble in BCD instead of only the nibble that needs it. Hex grouping runs from the right, not the left.
chapters.prereq: None; this chapter opens the unit.
chapters.leave: Adder and subtractor circuits to 5.4; code converters built from gates to 5.2.

chapters.idea: A logic gate is a switch network that computes one Boolean operation, and a few Boolean identities let you rewrite any function into a cheaper gate network.
chapters.depth: Symbols, truth tables and expressions for NOT, AND, OR, NAND, NOR, XOR and XNOR, in 2-input and 3-input forms; XOR as 'not equal' and as parity. Universal gates: NAND and NOR, each shown making NOT, AND and OR. De Morgan's two theorems and the bar-breaking rule. Identities with names: identity, null, idempotent, complement, involution, distributive, absorption A + AB = A, and A + A'B = A + B. Truth table to expression and expression to truth table. Cost measures: gate count and fan-in. Keep to two-level gate networks.

figure.aria: A tree with the NAND gate at the root and three branches showing NOT built from one NAND, AND from two NANDs and OR from three NANDs.

chapters.example: Reduce F = AB + A(B + C) + B(B + C) and realize the result with only 2-input NAND gates. Expand: F = AB + AB + AC + BB + BC = AB + AC + B + BC. Since B + BC = B, this is F = AB + AC + B, and AB is absorbed by B, so F = B + AC. NAND realization: N1 = NAND(A, C) gives (AC)'; N2 = NAND(B, B) gives B'; N3 = NAND(N2, N1) gives B + AC. Three 2-input NAND gates.
chapters.trap: De Morgan: when you break the bar you must change the sign, so (A + B)' = A'B' and not A' + B'. An XOR gate is not a universal gate.
chapters.prereq: 5.1 for the 0/1 bit patterns and the row order of a truth table.
chapters.leave: Systematic minimization to 5.3; gate-level adders to 5.4; feedback latches to 5.6.

chapters.idea: Every truth table has exactly one canonical sum-of-products and one canonical product-of-sums form, and a K-map removes the variables that change inside a group of adjacent cells.
chapters.depth: Minterm (a product term holding every variable once) and maxterm (a sum term holding every variable once), numbered by the binary value of their row. Canonical SOP written Σm(...), canonical POS written ΠM(...); the minterm list and maxterm list of one function are complements in index. K-map (Karnaugh map) layout for 2, 3 and 4 variables with rows and columns in Gray order 00, 01, 11, 10. Groups of 1, 2, 4 and 8 cells; top-bottom, left-right and corner adjacency. Prime and essential prime implicants in words only. Don't-care cells marked X, used only when they enlarge a group. SOP minimization by grouping 1s is the main exam method; POS minimization groups 0s and complements each variable (0 gives the variable, 1 gives its complement). A few syllabi call the map a Veitch diagram.

figure.title: K-map for F(A,B,C,D) = Σm(0,2,5,7,8,10,13,15)
figure.aria: A 4 by 4 K-map whose columns are CD = 00, 01, 11, 10, with the four corner cells marked as one group and the four middle cells marked as a second group.

chapters.example: Minimize F(A,B,C,D) = Σm(0,2,5,7,8,10,13,15) on a 4-variable K-map and give both the SOP and the POS form. The corners m0, m2, m8, m10 form one group: A and C change, B = 0 and D = 0, so the term is B'D'. The middle four m5, m7, m13, m15 form the second group: A and C change, B = 1 and D = 1, so the term is BD. SOP: F = B'D' + BD. Reading the 0s the same way gives F = (B + D')(B' + D).
chapters.trap: Writing the K-map rows and columns as 00, 01, 10, 11 instead of Gray order 00, 01, 11, 10, and forgetting that edges and corners are adjacent. In the POS method a 0 in the group gives the true variable and a 1 gives the complemented variable.
chapters.leave: Gate realization and gate counting to 5.2 and 5.4; putting an expression straight onto a multiplexer to 5.5.

chapters.idea: Adding two bits is itself a Boolean function, so an adder is the first useful combinational circuit built from the gates of 5.2.
chapters.depth: Half adder: truth table, S = A⊕B, C = AB, and the limitation that it has no carry input. Full adder: three inputs, S = A⊕B⊕Cin, Cout = AB + Cin(A⊕B), built from two half adders and one OR gate. 4-bit ripple-carry adder as four full adders chained by the carry, with carry propagation delay growing with the number of bits. BCD adder: a 4-bit binary adder plus correction logic that adds 0110 when the 4-bit sum is above 9 or the adder produces a carry-out; correction condition Cout + S3S2 + S3S1 where S3, S2, S1 are the top three sum bits. One worked two-digit BCD addition. Gate level only.

figure.title: Full adder from two half adders
figure.aria: A block flow where half adder 1 feeds half adder 2 with S1 and feeds the OR gate with C1, half adder 2 gives the sum and a second carry, and the OR gate gives the final carry.

chapters.example: Add 1011 and 0110 with a 4-bit ripple-carry adder, then add the BCD numbers 6 and 5 through a BCD adder. Ripple: bit 0 gives 1 + 0 = 1 with carry 0; bit 1 gives 1 + 1 = 0 with carry 1; bit 2 gives 0 + 1 + 1 = 0 with carry 1; bit 3 gives 1 + 0 + 1 = 0 with carry 1. The sum bits are 0001 with Cout = 1, so the answer is 1 0001 = 17, and 11 + 6 = 17. BCD: 0110 + 0101 = 1011 = 11, which is above 9, so add 0110: 1011 + 0110 = 1 0001, giving the nibbles 0001 0001 = 11.
chapters.trap: Cascading two half adders and forgetting the OR gate, so one carry is lost; and applying the BCD correction only to sums 10 to 15 while missing the carry-out case, as in 9 + 9.
chapters.prereq: 5.2 for XOR and AND gates; 5.3 for writing the correction condition; 5.1 for BCD codes.
chapters.leave: Subtraction and 2's complement arithmetic to 5.1; the adder inside a processor to 5.7.

chapters.idea: A multiplexer is a digitally controlled selector, and because each select code picks one input it can also hold a truth table and so implement any Boolean expression.
chapters.depth: 2:1 and 4:1 multiplexer (MUX, data selector): truth table, 2ⁿ inputs with n select lines, enable input. 4:1 built from three 2:1 multiplexers; 8:1 mentioned in one line. Implementing a Boolean function on a 4:1 multiplexer with two select lines, where the leftover variable ties each data input to 0, 1, C or C'. 1:4 demultiplexer (DEMUX, data distributor): truth table with one data input and two select lines; the decoder as the address-decoding part of a demux. Applications: parallel-to-serial conversion, routing signals onto a shared bus, driving a seven-segment display, and function generation.

figure.aria: A three-level tree where two 2:1 multiplexers with select S0 pick from input pairs I0, I1 and I2, I3, and a final 2:1 multiplexer with select S1 chooses between them.

chapters.example: Implement F(A,B,C) = Σm(1,2,6,7) on a 4:1 multiplexer with A and B as select lines. Group the truth table by AB. For AB = 00 the rows are m0 = 0 and m1 = 1, so I0 = C. For AB = 01 the rows are m2 = 1 and m3 = 0, so I1 = C'. For AB = 10 both rows are 0, so I2 = 0. For AB = 11 both rows are 1, so I3 = 1. Connect I0 = C, I1 = C', I2 = 0, I3 = 1, with A on the more significant select line S1 and B on S0.
chapters.trap: Swapping the select lines, since A must drive the more significant select pin, and forgetting that a 4:1 multiplexer has two select lines and four data inputs, so three variables cannot all go to the select pins.
chapters.prereq: 5.3 for truth tables and minterms; 5.2 for the internal AND-OR view of a multiplexer.
chapters.leave: Sequential selection and registers to 5.6; address decoding inside a chip to 5.7.

chapters.idea: A flip-flop stores one bit by feeding its own output back to its input, so the value stays after the input is removed.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this inside the introductory electrical and electronics unit, so keep it short and definition-based. Cross-coupled NOR SR latch with its truth table, including the forbidden S = R = 1 state; clocked SR latch. D flip-flop (output follows D at the active edge) and T flip-flop (toggles on every active edge). JK flip-flop truth table: hold, reset, set, toggle. Level triggering against edge triggering, and the race-around problem when J = K = 1 in a level-triggered JK. Characteristic table in one line, and a register as n flip-flops sharing one clock. Names to mention: latch, bistable multivibrator.

figure.title: Cross-coupled NOR SR latch
figure.aria: Two NOR gates wired as a loop: R drives NOR 1 whose Q output feeds NOR 2, S drives NOR 2 whose Q̄ output feeds back into NOR 1.

chapters.example: A positive edge-triggered JK flip-flop starts with Q = 0. Clock pulses arrive with (J,K) = (1,0), (1,1), (0,1), (1,1). Find Q after each pulse. Pulse 1: J = 1, K = 0 sets, so Q = 1. Pulse 2: J = K = 1 toggles, so Q = 0. Pulse 3: J = 0, K = 1 resets, so Q = 0. Pulse 4: J = K = 1 toggles, so Q = 1. Final state Q = 1 after four clock edges.
chapters.trap: Treating a transparent latch and an edge-triggered flip-flop as the same device, and expecting a level-triggered JK with J = K = 1 to toggle once per clock instead of many times during the high level.
chapters.prereq: 5.2 for NAND and NOR gates and feedback.
chapters.leave: Counters, shift registers and state-machine design to a later digital electronics course; CPU registers get one line in 5.7.

chapters.idea: A microprocessor is a CPU on a chip that needs memory and input/output built around it, while a microcontroller is that CPU with memory, timers and input/output pins on the same chip, made to control a device.
chapters.depth: Internal block diagram of a microprocessor: arithmetic logic unit, register file, program counter, instruction register, control unit, and the address, data and control buses; fetch-decode-execute cycle; clock and word length (8-bit, 16-bit, 32-bit). Von Neumann (one memory for program and data) against Harvard (separate program and data memory) in one line; CISC and RISC in one line. Microcontroller block: CPU plus Flash or ROM program memory, RAM, timers and counters, analog-to-digital converter, serial port (UART) and general purpose input/output (GPIO) ports. Use the 8051 family as the concrete chip: 8-bit CPU, 4 KB program memory, 128 bytes RAM, 32 input/output pins, two 16-bit timers. Define an embedded system, with applications: washing machine, microwave oven, air-conditioner, car engine control, energy meter, traffic light. No instruction set.

figure.title: Inside a microcontroller chip
figure.aria: A single chip drawn as a system bus at the top with seven blocks hanging from it: CPU core, Flash memory, RAM, timers, ADC, GPIO pins and serial UART.

chapters.example: A washing machine must read a water-level sensor, run the motor for a set time and light an LED when the cycle ends. Name the blocks used and choose between a microprocessor and a microcontroller. The sensor needs an analog-to-digital converter input; the set time needs a timer; the motor and LED need GPIO output pins driving a relay and a driver transistor. A microcontroller such as the 8051 family fits on one board: 8-bit CPU, 4 KB program memory, 128 bytes RAM, two 16-bit timers, 32 input/output pins. A microprocessor would need separate ROM, RAM, timer and ADC chips plus far more wiring, so the microcontroller wins on cost, size and power.
chapters.trap: Swapping the definitions, for example claiming a microprocessor has RAM and timers on chip or that a microcontroller has no program memory. Clock speed in MHz alone does not fix the work done, because one instruction may take several clock cycles.
chapters.prereq: 5.2 for the ALU as a gate network, 5.4 for the adder inside it, 5.5 for bus selection, 5.6 for registers.
chapters.leave: Analog-to-digital converter circuits and comparators to Unit 4; sensors and transducers to Unit 6; assembly language and instruction timing to a later course.
